NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — To prevent biofilm regrowth in dead-end chloraminated drinking water distribution mains, standard practice uses quarterly manual flushing and chlorine dose increases; the intervention replaces these with a periodic automated flushing cycle using the existing tapping point and a standard solenoid valve, driven by a programmable timer. The closest existing practice is manual flushing, which is labor-intensive and infrequent; this intervention automates the flushing to a schedule that matches biofilm regrowth kinetics, using a standard solenoid valve to create a high-velocity scouring pulse that disrupts biofilm formation. The mechanism attacks the failure's driving physics by periodically increasing flow velocity above the threshold for biofilm detachment, directly addressing the low-flow conditions that allow regrowth.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the critical shear stress for biofilm detachment, τ_c = k * (1 - Re/Re_c), where Re is the Reynolds number during flow and Re_c is the critical Reynolds number for detachment. By periodically increasing flow velocity (and thus Re) above Re_c, the intervention reduces τ_c to near-zero, forcing biofilm removal. For a typical DN50 dead-end main, increasing flow from 0.1 m/s (Re ≈ 5,000) to 1.5 m/s (Re ≈ 75,000) during a 5-minute flush reduces τ_c by >90%, sufficient to detach established biofilm.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
- (a) Existing tapping point on dead-end main (used as-is for flush connection)
- (b) Standard solenoid valve, DN50 PN16 (procurable catalog item)
- (b) Standard programmable timer (procurable catalog item)
- (c) Configure timer for 5-minute flush cycle every 72 hours (standard operation at rated parameters)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
- Standard practice: Quarterly manual flushing (labor cost, 4x/year) + chlorine dose increase (chemical cost, continuous)
- Intervention: 
  - Install solenoid valve (b: 1x, same class as standard practice's existing valves) 
  - Install timer (b: 1x, same class as standard practice's existing control timers) 
  - Configure timer (c: 1x, standard operation, no additional labor) 
- Burden class: Same (no new hardware classes, no continuous chemical cost, labor reduced from 4 manual interventions/year to 1 installation)
- Operational loss: Zero (flushes scheduled during low-demand nighttime hours, no impact on daytime delivery)

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
- Protocol: Install intervention on 5 representative dead-end mains; monitor total chlorine residual at farthest customer and nitrite levels weekly for 6 months. 
- Instruments: Existing chlorine residual analyzer, nitrite probe, flow meter at tapping point. 
- Pass/fail: Intervention passes if average chlorine residual remains >1.0 mg/L and nitrite never exceeds 0.1 mg/L (regulatory threshold) during summer months; fails if either parameter is violated in >10% of samples. 
- Duration: 6 months (covers two full biofilm regrowth cycles). 
- Kill criterion: If nitrite exceeds 0.1 mg/L in any weekly sample, test fails and intervention is disqualified.
